grades: Doctrines, claims, hero appointments and cards have consequences. Engaged automation survives almost twice as many waves as declining; this does not establish several equally viable expert plans.
Terrain, focus, governors, logistics and markets interact. Extra economic activity produced much more gold but only a small, noisy survival improvement in this probe.
Routes, supply connections, loyalty and military travel already matter. The interface could make route value, arrival time and opportunity cost easier to compare.
Five formations, stances, stamina, moments, withdrawal and command delegation create a promising decision space. Late escalation also shortens reading windows and removes help.
Strong art and useful aftermath coexist with a composite POWER beside a different THREAT quantity, mixed progression labels and a confirmed “certain”/53% contradiction.
Rich identity creation precedes the strategic hook; an empty inheritance sheet still appears on the first reign. A quick coronation path and contextual Copilot already exist.
The court and combat have useful rhythm, but the played opening repeatedly interrupted preparation. Desktop Hands-on suppresses routine prompts; that changes pacing as well as control.
Legacy, Dynasty and Cabinet give continuity. Their overlapping levels, duplicates and loadouts make it difficult to tell which reward changes this run.
Seeds, heroes, cards, stories and waves provide variety. Main Ascent is endless, with defeat and inheritance rather than a selectable campaign victory contract.
Phone controls use a compact dock; desktop has a map with side sheets, keys and manual orders. Stable shortcuts, comparisons and measured touch ergonomics can improve both.
Vietnamese history, named characters and Đông Hồ print art give a coherent identity worth preserving. This is the clearest product differentiator.
Save/resume and pauses exist. Late-game assistance overrides and small combat annotations are concrete concerns; physical-device performance and assistive access remain unverified.

loops.title: Keep combat readable as mastery rises
loops.idea: Add more speed and hide the counter guide in late waves, so experienced players must react and remember.
loops.critique: The current game already does this. Wave 13 enforces fast pace; later steps cap speech, raise enemy difficulty and hide assistance. Success can make the interface less accessible. Memorizing a ring is a different skill from choosing when to spend stamina.
loops.tune: Separate enemy competence, combat speed and reading assistance. Retain the player’s slow pace, explicit counter guide and optional automatic pause at a decision.
loops.challenge: Unlimited stopping could remove time pressure for players who enjoy it. A globally slower battle could also make ordinary fights drag.
loops.final: Ship independent settings: enemy difficulty, pace, readable intent, and pause-on-moment. Keep a clearly chosen timed challenge preset. Use stronger enemy plans and fewer safe responses to raise strategic difficulty; preserve assistance in normal runs.
loops.measure: At wave 20+, the selected slow speed and guide remain effective. In usability tests, at least 80% can explain the next enemy action before choosing a response. Treat that percentage as a target to test, not an existing result.

loops.title: A reign should sometimes end in triumph
loops.idea: Add a victory at wave 12, then end every run.
loops.critique: A mandatory cutoff would truncate a strong build. A fixed wave count also treats exploration, diplomacy and defence as the same achievement.
loops.tune: Offer a finite charter with a wave horizon and one thematic goal, followed by a choice to bank the result or continue.
loops.challenge: Stacking several objectives can turn a relaxing phone run into a checklist. Banking too early may become the optimal progression farm.
loops.final: Prototype one short charter: hold the capital through the first great invasion and preserve one chosen border. The initial candidate is the first four waves, tuned by observed wall-clock sessions. Award a complete ending; offer a second chapter or Endless. Later charters can emphasize trade or alliances. Normalize rewards by difficulty and meaningful milestones.
loops.measure: Candidate mobile chapter: 8–12 minutes including reading; desktop extended reign: 20–35 minutes. These are hypotheses. Keep only if players understand the goal and at least 70% of finishers want another chapter or a new build.

loops.title: Preparation needs uninterrupted space
loops.idea: Remove most court cards and let autopilot handle the economy.
loops.critique: Cards are currently the main way many phone players exercise agency. Removing them would turn a grand strategy game into watching the simulation.
loops.tune: Queue routine advice in a compact court inbox; interrupt for danger, an expiring commitment or a genuinely new rule.
loops.challenge: An inbox can become an invisible backlog. Too much batching can make all strategy happen in one exhausting menu.
loops.final: Use the existing Aftermath → Court → Muster → Field structure. Present one strategic headline and up to three optional queued decisions. Pause for urgent, irreversible choices. Allow the player to pull any lane on demand. Let doctrine handle repeat maintenance under visible reserve budgets.
loops.measure: Target no more than two unsolicited full-screen decisions between ordinary waves after onboarding. Measure decision comprehension, ignored important events and actions per completed objective—not simply fewer taps.

loops.title: Make growth feel like an advantage
loops.idea: Remove all enemy adaptation and all price scaling.
loops.critique: The current game uses several bounded controllers, not a single unlimited rubber band. Removing everything could produce idle snowballs and trivial late-game purchases.
loops.tune: Publish the base wave, ambition, rival pressure and adaptive portion; lock a visible wave budget before the player finishes preparing.
loops.challenge: A player may exploit the lock by hoarding strength until after the snapshot. Full formulas on a phone would be unreadable.
loops.final: First instrument each contribution and run matched policy experiments. Prototype a muster snapshot with a bounded adaptation envelope. Count committed recruitment and construction when appropriate. Keep a short front forecast with a detail drill-down. Demand a measurable benefit from successful preparation before retuning all prices.
loops.measure: On the same scenario, a sensible defensive investment should improve losses, territory held or capital safety in a large majority of cases. Pre-register an 80% directional target and inspect exceptions. Compare outcomes as well as the displayed POWER.

loops.title: Build identity from interactions
loops.idea: Add dozens of new cards, units and building levels.
loops.critique: There are already 52 card definitions, 22 eligible for normal drafts and eight opening boons. More content may dilute the chance of forming a coherent plan and multiply balance work.
loops.tune: Audit the existing pool for three viable engines: fortified food/logistics, trading diplomacy, and mobile expansion. Give each a visible strength and a failure case.
loops.challenge: Rigid engines could make drafts solved recipes; forced card bundles would reduce improvisation.
loops.final: Keep flexible bridges between engines. Prototype two interaction changes within the existing pool before expanding it. A food surplus might support a reserve host but face wage pressure; trade can fund defence but needs safe connections; expansion opens resources but stretches supply. Clearly mark proposed interactions that do not exist yet.
loops.measure: Across 32–64 seeds and several competent policies, no starter engine should dominate every map. Players should name their build and its weakness after the second draft. Rework generic upgrades that cannot change a decision.

loops.title: One simulation, two comfortable ways to command
loops.idea: Give desktop players more compulsory micromanagement than mobile players.
loops.critique: Desktop already starts with Hands-on enabled, disabling autopilot and routine lane prompts. More chores are not automatically more depth, and platform defaults can conceal that this is a rules change.
loops.tune: Share the economic and combat rules. Let players choose Guided command or Hands-on command on either platform, with clear explanations and easy switching.
loops.challenge: An expert workspace can overwhelm a phone; automation must not silently override explicit orders or make experts irrelevant.
loops.final: Mobile uses intent presets, single-province drill-down and one urgent front at a time. Desktop adds pinned comparisons, stable shortcuts, routes, queues and optional multi-host selection. Both expose reserve budgets, order precedence and the same consequences. Prototype the command workspace with existing armies before adding units.
loops.measure: A desktop player can compare two fronts and queue a response in under 20 seconds after learning the controls. A mobile player can give an equivalent strategic intention in at most three major taps. Validate, do not assume, both targets.

loops.title: Make inheritance rewarding without obscuring skill
loops.idea: Merge Legacy, Dynasty and Cabinet into one universal currency.
loops.critique: A hard merge would discard distinct rewards and disrupt existing saves. Removing progression power overnight could make earned collections feel devalued.
loops.tune: Unify the explanation and end-of-run presentation while keeping the underlying stores. Distinguish permanent collection level, this-run stack and current-reign experience.
loops.challenge: A prettier reward screen alone does not resolve grinding or fresh-profile disadvantage.
loops.final: Use one inheritance summary: what was earned, what changed, and one optional next-run choice. Add a normalized challenge preset with clearly defined progression treatment. Prefer new options and sidegrades for future rewards; preserve existing ownership and test any balance migration separately.
loops.measure: At least 80% of testers can identify which of three rewards affects the next run, this run or collection completion. Compare new and progressed profiles with identical decision policies.

loops.title: Turn defeat into a useful next attempt
loops.idea: Add a detailed log explaining every multiplier after a loss.
loops.critique: There is already an aftermath and chronicle. A huge ledger may explain the engine while failing to help a disappointed player decide what to try next.
loops.tune: Show the decisive timeline: arrival, supply failure, formation exchange, reinforcement or capital loss. Offer one plausible alternative with an uncertainty label.
loops.challenge: A counterfactual can be wrong when changing an order changes later random events. Automatic advice can sound falsely certain or blame the player.
loops.final: Start with facts from the event log: “Relief arrived two seasons after contact.” Add a bounded comparison only where it can be simulated consistently. Let players replay a practice snapshot when feasible. Lead with the story and one learnable cause; keep the detailed ledger optional.
loops.measure: After a loss, at least 70% can name one specific adjustment for the next attempt. Verify every factual explanation against recorded events. Do not fabricate precise alternate win chances.

loops.title: Make Vietnamese strategy part of the rules
loops.idea: Build a full naval layer, historical campaign map and many new factions immediately.
loops.critique: That scope would compete with the current game’s clarity and balance problems. New movement, combat and economy layers would require extensive teaching and art.
loops.tune: Use existing formations, terrain, supply and character stories for a small historical scenario with a distinct tactical problem.
loops.challenge: A famous battle becomes a trivia skin if the winning action is unchanged; a scripted historical win can remove agency.
loops.final: Prototype one river-crossing or prepared-ground encounter. Telegraph its rule, allow more than one solution, and make a retreat/bait plan costly if mistimed. Keep historical framing separate from invented procedural outcomes. Expand only if this encounter changes players’ decisions and remains legible on a phone.
loops.measure: Players should describe the scenario’s terrain rule without opening a codex and use at least two successful approaches. Reuse existing systems before introducing a full navy.
